title: Three perfect days in Prague
dek: Candles on the graves, a queen's portrait show at the foot of the Castle, Debussy at the National Theatre and the last farmers' market of October on the river: Prague turns inward, and it suits the city.

hero.caption: Charles Bridge and the Malá Strana towers, the walk you will make more than once this weekend.

intro:
Prague's clocks went back an hour on Sunday, October 25, and the city has settled into its short-day rhythm: dark by late afternoon, cafés full by four, the river steaming in the cold. This is the weekend of **Dušičky**, the Czech days of the dead. All Saints' Day falls on Sunday, All Souls' on Monday, and from Saturday the city's cemeteries stay open until 19:00 so families can bring candles and wreaths. At Vyšehrad and in the long avenues of Olšany the effect after dusk is quiet and very beautiful, and visitors are welcome as long as they behave like guests.

Halloween is here too, mostly as a bar-crawl import, but the better party is Mexican: the Náprstek Museum's free **Día de Muertos** fills Betlémské náměstí with altars, mariachi and Catrinas on Saturday and Sunday. The National Gallery has just opened *Anne Jagiellon (1503–1547)*, a big Renaissance show in the Wallenstein Riding School, and Kunsthalle Praha has Annette Messager's first major Prague retrospective. At the National Theatre, Christof Loy's new *Pelléas et Mélisande* has its first post-premiere night on Saturday, and Balanchine's *Who Cares?* plays the State Opera all weekend.

The forecast calls for light rain on Friday and a wet Saturday afternoon, then a drier Sunday, so the plan keeps the long outdoor stretches for the mornings and for Sunday, with museums and warm rooms in between. Pack a proper coat and shoes for cobbles. Independence Day was Wednesday, October 28, so this weekend carries no public holiday: shops and museums keep normal hours, and Sunday is quieter than Saturday.

days.title: Friday: the Castle and Malá Strana
days.intro: A day under the Castle, mostly indoors as the drizzle comes and goes, ending in two of the best beer rooms on the left bank.

stops.name: Café Savoy
stops.text: Start under the painted neo-Renaissance ceiling of Café Savoy, at the river end of Malá Strana by the Legion Bridge. Bread and pastries are baked on the premises every day, and the café works with the Myšák confectionery on its desserts, so take something from the counter with your coffee, or settle in for a full breakfast. It opens at 08:00 on weekdays, so on Friday you will beat the brunch crowd. From here, tram 22 or 23 climbs to the Castle in a few minutes.

stops.name: Prague Castle and St. Vitus Cathedral
stops.text: Do the Castle early, before the tour groups pile up. The basic circuit (450 CZK, valid for two days) covers St. Vitus Cathedral, the Old Royal Palace with its vaulted Vladislav Hall, St. George's Basilica and Golden Lane. The cathedral is the reason to come; look for the Mucha window in the north nave. The buildings are open 09:00 to 17:00 and the courtyards much longer, so you can come back after dark. Buy tickets online through Ticketportal or at the information centres in the second and third courtyards.

stops.name: Kuchyň
stops.text: Just outside the Castle gates, through the terrace of the Salm Palace, Kuchyň ("kitchen") cooks Czech home food with a daily menu, an open kitchen where you watch the cooks, and carefully kept tank Pilsner. The view over the red roofs of Malá Strana is one of the best in town, even under grey skies. Order the duck with bread dumplings, or whatever braise is on the board. It is open daily from 11:30, and booking is wise on a Friday.

stops.name: Anne Jagiellon at the Wallenstein Riding School
stops.text: Walk down the Old Castle Stairs to the National Gallery's new exhibition, which opened on October 22. *Anne Jagiellon (1503–1547): Queen at the Dawn of a New Era* marks 500 years since the Habsburgs took the Bohemian throne through her marriage to Ferdinand I. More than 200 loans, with works by Cranach, Dürer and Titian, tell the story of a queen with fifteen children and a court that remade Prague Castle in the Renaissance. Her letters carry the private side. Open Tuesday to Sunday, 10:00 to 18:00.

stops.name: Kunsthalle Praha: Annette Messager
stops.text: A few minutes away, by Malostranská station, Kunsthalle Praha occupies a former electrical substation and stays open until 21:00 on Fridays. *Tragikomedie* is a large solo show of the French artist Annette Messager, whose fifty-year practice turns fabric, toys and stuffed animals into what the gallery calls "fragile monuments to memory, identity, and desire." It is tender and unsettling in equal parts, which is just right for Halloween weekend. Tickets are 320 CZK, and the show runs to February.

stops.name: Lokál U Bílé kuželky
stops.text: Below the Malá Strana end of Charles Bridge, this branch of the Lokál chain is a real beer hall in vaulted rooms, and it is where locals bring visitors to show them how Pilsner Urquell should be poured. Order a *šnyt*, a glass with a deep head of foam, to see the technique, then fried cheese with tartar sauce and buttered potatoes, or the pork neck. If the front room is packed, go down the stairs by the kitchen to the cellar. Open until 01:00 on Fridays.

stops.name: U Hrocha
stops.text: Finish on a steep lane under the Castle at U Hrocha ("At the Hippo"), a small pub in a fifteenth-century house with shared tables, plain wooden furniture and only one beer: Pilsner Urquell. The service is famously brusque; do not take it personally. Order *pivní sýr*, beer cheese with paprika, onion and butter that you mash together and spread on bread, and let a stranger slide in beside you. Open daily until 23:30.

days.title: Saturday: the river, Vyšehrad and the Old Town
days.intro: Market breakfast on the embankment, candles at Vyšehrad before the rain sets in, a Mexican day of the dead in the Old Town, and Debussy at night.

stops.name: Náplavka Farmers' Market
stops.text: The Saturday market on the embankment by Palackého most is in its seventeenth season and runs every week until December 19, 08:00 to 14:00. Come early for breakfast standing up: coffee, sourdough, sausages, cheese from small dairies, apple juice and, at this time of year, warm cider and the last of the pumpkins. The barges moored below the quay give it a lazy look even in the cold. The Dancing House is a five-minute walk upriver if you want a photograph.

stops.name: Vyšehrad and its cemetery
stops.text: Walk south along the river for twenty minutes and climb to Vyšehrad, the old fortress on the rock. Go first to the cemetery by the Basilica of St. Peter and St. Paul: Dvořák, Smetana, Mucha and Karel Čapek lie here, and the Slavín pantheon holds the national greats. On Dušičky weekend the graves fill with candles and wreaths, and the cemetery stays open until 19:00. The basilica itself is open from 10:00 (130 CZK). Then walk the ramparts for the view down the Vltava.

stops.name: U Kroka
stops.text: Just below the Vyšehrad walls, U Kroka is a neighbourhood restaurant that does Czech cooking properly. Start with *česnečka*, garlic soup, which earns its reputation, then pork knee roasted in dark lager, bacon-wrapped rabbit loin or pork cheeks in red wine. Portions are generous, so share if you are going to the opera tonight. It is open daily from 11:30, with the kitchen closed between 16:00 and 17:00. Book on a Saturday; it fills with families.

stops.name: Día de Muertos at the Náprstek Museum
stops.text: When the afternoon rain arrives, take the tram from Výtoň to Národní třída and walk to Betlémské náměstí, where the Náprstek Museum of Asian, African and American Cultures holds its free Mexican Day of the Dead on Saturday and Sunday, 10:00 to 21:30. Expect decorated *ofrendas* for the dead, Mariachi Azteca de Praga, folk dance, Mexican craft stalls, workshops and a Catrina contest, with a procession of painted faces through the Old Town. It is the most cheerful way to mark the weekend.

stops.name: Café Louvre
stops.text: A long first-floor café on Národní třída with more than a century of history, high ceilings, and waiters who have seen everything. It is three minutes from the National Theatre, which makes it the right place for an early dinner before the curtain: schnitzel or goulash from the Czech side of the menu, a glass of Moravian wine, then apple strudel if you have time. Open until 23:30, so you could also come back after the show.

stops.name: Pelléas et Mélisande at the National Theatre
stops.text: Christof Loy's new production of Debussy's opera opened on October 15, and Saturday is its next performance, with Patrick Fournillier conducting the National Theatre orchestra. It is a dreamlike, slow-burning piece about love and jealousy in a dark castle, which suits a late-autumn night, and the gilded house built by public subscription is worth seeing for itself. Sung in French with Czech and English surtitles; about three and a half hours with two intervals, so you will be out around 22:30.

days.title: Sunday: Vinohrady, Žižkov and All Saints
days.intro: The driest day of the three, spent east of the center: a Plečnik church, Kafka's grave, and Olšany as the candles come on.

stops.name: Bistro Café Laskavá
stops.text: Vinohrady is Prague's best neighbourhood for a slow Sunday, all tall apartment houses and tree-lined streets, and its brunch scene keeps changing. Laskavá is one of the steady names: good cold cuts and butter, open sourdough sandwiches, eggs done several ways, and homemade cakes. Hours are not posted widely, so check before you go, and if it is full, Grøn next door does lighter plates.

stops.name: Church of the Most Sacred Heart of Our Lord
stops.wiki: Church of the Most Sacred Heart of Our Lord
stops.text: Josip Plečnik's church of 1928 to 1932 is the strangest and best building in Vinohrady: a brick and granite hall often compared to Noah's ark, with a tower the full width of the façade and a glass clock 7.6 metres across. On All Saints' Day there are Masses at 09:00 and 11:00, and the church opens 45 minutes before each one; you can sit quietly at the back. Otherwise the vestibule, with a view of the interior, is open 09:00 to 17:00.

stops.name: Vinohradský pivovar
stops.text: Ten minutes' walk east, the neighbourhood brewery reopened in 2014 in the vaulted cellars of the old Vinohrady burghers' brewery, founded in 1893. Half the cellar holds the brewing kit, the rest a taproom and restaurant. Drink the house 11° or 12° lager or the amber Jantar 13°, and eat modern Czech pub food: venison with bread dumplings, cream sauce and cranberries if it is on, or the soft sausages to share. Open Sunday 11:00 to 22:00.

stops.name: New Jewish Cemetery and Kafka's grave
stops.text: Take tram or metro a few stops east to Želivského. The New Jewish Cemetery is a green, ivy-hung place, and Franz Kafka is buried here with his parents under a pale hexagonal stone (grave 21-14-21), with a plaque to his friend Max Brod opposite. Entry is free. From November the cemetery closes at 16:00 on Sundays, so do not linger over lunch; it is closed on Saturdays and Jewish holidays.

stops.name: Olšany Cemetery at dusk
stops.text: Walk west into Olšany, the city's largest cemetery, laid out after the plague of 1680 and now a maze of chestnut avenues, leaning stones and ivy. On All Saints' Day it is full of Prague families tending graves, and as the sun goes down a little after half past four the lanterns come on across the whole hillside. Jan Palach is buried here. The gates stay open until 19:00 all weekend; walk slowly, keep your voice down and leave photographs of strangers' grief alone.

stay.name: Mandarin Oriental, Prague
stay.text: On a quiet lane in Malá Strana, a short walk from Café Savoy and five minutes from Charles Bridge, so Friday's whole route is on foot and the Castle is a climb away. The spa is a real asset on a wet weekend.

stay.name: Hotel Paris Prague
stay.text: A 1904 hotel in Art Nouveau and Gothic Revival style next to the Municipal House, run by the same family for three generations. It puts the Old Town, the Estates Theatre and the metro to Vinohrady all within easy reach.

stay.name: Mosaic House
stay.text: A design hotel on Odborů within a short walk of Náplavka and the National Theatre, which makes Saturday easy. There is a café open from 08:00 to 23:30, a courtyard garden and a private sauna to book after the cemetery walks.

events.name: Who Cares? (Czech National Ballet)
events.when: Fri. and Sat. 7 p.m.; Sun. 5 p.m.
events.text: Balanchine's Gershwin ballet, paired with his *Brahms-Schoenberg Quartet*, in a double bill of about 1 hour 50 minutes in the restored State Opera by the National Museum.

events.name: Náplavka Farmers' Market
events.text: The weekly riverside market, running every Saturday through December 19: produce, bread, cheese, street food and hot drinks.

events.name: Día de Muertos at the Náprstek Museum
events.when: Sat. and Sun. 10 a.m. to 9:30 p.m.
events.text: Free Mexican Day of the Dead with altars, mariachi, dance, crafts, workshops, a Catrina contest and a procession through the Old Town.

events.name: "Tichá sláva Vyšehradu": Dušičky tour of Vyšehrad and Slavín
events.text: A guided walk (in Czech) through the cemetery including the Slavín crypt, led by Václav Liška and Alena Lehnerová of the Svatobor society, part of the city cemeteries' All Souls program.

events.name: Pelléas et Mélisande
events.text: Christof Loy's new staging of Debussy, conducted by Patrick Fournillier, with Arnheiður Eiríksdóttir as Mélisande. French with Czech and English surtitles.

events.name: Bohemians Praha 1905 v. Sparta Praha
events.text: Neither Sparta nor Slavia is at home this weekend, but Sparta cross town to Bohemians' small, loud ground in Vršovice for a round 13 Chance Liga derby.

events.name: Le nozze di Figaro
events.text: Mozart in the theatre where *Don Giovanni* had its premiere, a short metro ride from Olšany if you want to end Sunday in the Old Town.

events.name: Olšany: the cemetery as a space between worlds
events.where: Olšany Cemeteries, meeting at the Infocentrum
events.text: A guided Dušičky walk with Kateřina Pavlitová (200 CZK, booked through GoOut). The evening candlelit walks on Friday and Monday are already sold out.

know: **From the airport:** bus 59 runs from Václav Havel Airport to Nádraží Veleslavín on metro line A in about 35 minutes, and bus 100 to Zličín on line B in about 45; both take an ordinary 90-minute ticket (46 CZK in the app, 50 CZK on paper). The Airport Express (AE) goes to the main station, Hlavní nádraží, in about 45 minutes for 200 CZK; passes are not valid on it. A taxi, Uber or Bolt to the center usually takes 25 to 40 minutes, depending on traffic.

**Transit:** buy tickets in the PID Lítačka app, which is cheapest: 36 CZK for 30 minutes, 46 CZK for 90 minutes, 140 CZK for 24 hours, 340 CZK for 72 hours. Activate a ticket before you board and keep it on your phone; fines for riding without one are steep.

**Tram works:** the track between I. P. Pavlova and Otakarova is closed through Sunday, November 1, affecting lines 2, 6, 11, 13 and 21, and Jana Želivského street in Žižkov has no trams until December 18 (bus X9 replaces them). Use metro A to Flora or Želivského for Olšany.
**The clock change:** Czech clocks went back an hour on October 25, so it is dark by about 16:45. Plan outdoor sightseeing for the mornings, and check that your phone has updated.

**Dušičky manners:** cemeteries stay open 08:00 to 19:00 from Saturday through Monday. Visitors are welcome, but this is a family occasion: keep quiet, do not move candles, and photograph the light, not the mourners.

**Money:** the currency is the Czech koruna (CZK), not the euro. Cards and phone payments are accepted almost everywhere, including most pubs, but carry some cash for market stalls. If euros are offered at a shop or exchange, decline; the rate is poor.
**Tipping:** service is not usually included. Round up or add about 10 percent in restaurants and cafés, and tell the server the total you want to pay when they bring the card machine.
**Hours:** Museums mostly close on Mondays (Kunsthalle Praha closes on Tuesdays instead). There is no public holiday this weekend, so shops keep normal Saturday and Sunday hours.
